Split the conjunction.

For the first statement, separate the case \(x=0\). Otherwise \(h_0\) gives \(y\neq0\). Set \(z=x-y\). Orthogonality gives
\[
\langle x,z\rangle=\|x\|^2,\qquad
\|z\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2.
\]
Use the inner-product characterization of the angle between \(x\) and \(z\), together with the Pythagorean identity, to obtain
\[
\tan(\angle(x,z))=\frac{\|y\|}{\|x\|}.
\]
Nonvanishing of \(x\) and \(y\) handles the required divisions. The \(x=0\) branch follows from the library’s conventions for angles involving the zero vector and division by zero.

For the second statement, unfold membership in the perpendicular bisector as equality of distances. Point reflection about \(p_2\) sends \(p_1\) to the point whose displacement from \(p_2\) is
\[
-(p_1-p_2).
\]
Expanding the two squared distances from \(c\), their equality reduces by polarization to
\[
\langle c-p_2,\;p_1-p_2\rangle=0.
\]
Thus the main useful intermediate goal is the standard “equidistant from two symmetric points iff orthogonal to their joining direction” characterization, after simplifying the `pointReflection` displacement identities.
